topic: BAML Structured Outputs False Confidence Guide 2026

competitors.title: Structured Outputs Create False Confidence
key_points: Constrained decoding forces models to prioritize output conformance over output quality — structured outputs often degrade response quality compared to free-form text APIs
GPT-5.2 with structured outputs returned banana quantity as 1.0 instead of 0.46 on a receipt extraction task; the same model with completions API returned the correct 0.46
Chain-of-thought reasoning is crippled by structured outputs — models forced into JSON can't reason step-by-step without escaping newlines and special characters
Schema ambiguity problems: what error type for an elephant picture? What about partial receipt parses? The more you enumerate errors, the more the LLM hallucinates errors (pink elephant problem)
BAML's solution: schema-aligned parsing (SAP) — a forgiving parser that coerces unquoted strings, missing brackets, wrong types into the correct schema without constrained decoding penalties

competitors.title: BAML Documentation — What is BAML?
key_points: BAML is a domain-specific language for generating structured outputs from LLMs — with first-class VSCode/Cursor/JetBrains/Zed IDE support
Type-safe outputs: define classes in BAML syntax, generate baml_client in Python/TypeScript/Ruby/Go/Rust, get autocomplete and compile-time validation
Schema-Aligned Parsing (SAP): patented technique that outperforms OpenAI's constrained decoding on Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard — gpt-3.5-turbo achieved 92% with SAP vs 87.5% with native FC
Model-agnostic: works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, OpenRouter, vLLM — no need to wait for model-specific structured output support
Built-in VSCode Playground for testing prompts without burning tokens on API calls, with hot-reload and full prompt preview

competitors.title: Prompting vs JSON Mode vs Function Calling vs Constrained Generation vs SAP
key_points: Nine techniques compared for structured data extraction: naive prompting, prompt engineering, prompt engineering + parsing, JSON mode, constrained generation, function calling, LLM retries, AST parsing, and SAP
SAP achieves 94.4% accuracy on BFCL with claude-3-5-sonnet vs 78.1% for function calling and 93.8% for Python AST parsing
Constrained generation forces models into token-level restrictions that can degrade output quality — SAP instead allows flexible output and corrects at parse time
All techniques classified into three categories: prompt changes, model/token changes, and parser changes — only SAP addresses the parser category without constraining the model

competitors.title: Your Prompts Are Using 4x More Tokens Than You Need
key_points: Type-definitions (like TypeScript interfaces) use 60% fewer tokens than JSON schemas for the same schema, with no information loss
JSON schemas with $defs, anyOf, and nested refs bloat prompts — a 4-element order schema went from 56 tokens (JSON schema) to 14 tokens (type-definitions)
Complex nested schemas with descriptions and enums: JSON schema was 66% more tokens than type-definitions
On GPT-4 this means 1600 API calls vs 400 calls for the same budget — 4x cost savings
Type-definitions are more readable and debuggable; easier to identify errors in schema definitions

competitors.title: Say What You Mean: A Response to 'Let Me Speak Freely' (dottxt / Outlines)
key_points: Structured generation does NOT degrade performance — properly implemented structured generation (Outlines) improves accuracy across GSM8K (0.77→0.78), Last Letter (0.73→0.77), and Shuffle Object (0.41→0.44) tasks
The 'Let Me Speak Freely' paper used fundamentally flawed methodology: different prompts for structured vs unstructured, and used an 'AI Parser' (Claude) to parse unstructured output
The AI Parser was doing the heavy lifting — flexible regex outperformed it (0.61 vs 0.57) and is cheaper/faster
Key lesson: structured generation is running your response parser as a generator — unify the prompt, parser, and structure for best results

competitors.title: LLMs Do Not Understand Numbers
key_points: Stop asking LLMs to add confidence scores, sum receipt items, or count rows in PDFs — they are fundamentally bad at numerical reasoning
GPT-5.1 correctly counts R's in 'strawberry' but refuses or returns wrong counts for larger tasks (claimed 82 function definitions but only returned 68 names)
OpenAI trained refusal associations for counting tasks — this reinforces the model's numerical weaknesses rather than solving them
Implication for structured outputs: don't design schemas that require the LLM to perform arithmetic or counting to fill in fields accurately
